title: Ilhan Omar investigation: Judge initially blocked DOJ from searching congresswoman’s home | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

A federal magistrate judge refused to allow the Justice Department to search Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC, house last month without taking precautions because she is a member of Congress, court filings made public this week confirm.

The court records show that Judge Matthew Sharbaugh forced DOJ to revise the plan for its search of Omar’s home in court proceedings over seven days in early October.

The search, which Sharbaugh ultimately authorized, took place on October 12.CNN previously reportedthat the judge had limited how federal investigators could access Omar’s house and records. The exact protocol ultimately proposed by DOJ and then approved by Sharbaugh remains under seal.

“The government can still pursue criminal investigations against Members of Congress, and it can still secure and execute search warrants along the lines contemplated here,” Sharbaugh wrote in October, according to the unsealed court records. “It simply must do so while fairly balancing the legislative interests by allowing the Congressperson targeted by any such search warrant an opportunity to identify any protected material before the search, subject to potential further scrutiny and review by the courts, if necessary.”

The records were unsealed in the DC District Court after CNN, the New York Times, more than a dozen other news outlets and the conservative transparency group Judicial Watch argued for transparency in the case.

The Minnesota congresswoman hasn’t been charged with any crime, and the court records have redacted all mentions of what she is being investigated for and the DOJ’s description of the evidence it had to merit the search.

The filings also capture an unusual and extreme argument the Justice Department made, and which Sharbaugh rejected: That Omar was unlikely to have taken home her legislative work, because people rarely have printed work product because of the internet, and her Capitol Hill office was close by. Thus, prosecutors said, special considerations for her Constitutional protections weren’t needed in a search of her private residence.

But the judge said otherwise.

“A Member’s legislative work is not limited to banker’s hours,” Sharbaugh wrote. “And a Member’s legislative work is not nearly cabined to the four walls of their Congressional office. More so than many vocations, the work of a Congressperson occurs in many different settings in many different places at many different times.”

Prosecutors argued that the House general counsel — currently chosen by Republican congressional leadership — sided with them as well, saying that a search of a lawmaker’s private residence didn’t require extra precautions to protect the members’ Constitutional protections from the Speech or Debate Clause, which walls off legislative work and records from criminal cases.

DC District Chief Judge James Boasberg is still looking at whether more of the court record around the search of Omar should be made public.

Several Trump administration officials have publicly said Omar is under investigation for immigration fraud, including lying about her age — allegations which she denies.

The records released this week say investigators were searching for paper documents, electronic data, and other items dating back to 1980 that could factor into the investigation. Omar, a naturalized US citizen who fled Somalia as a child, maintains she was born in 1982.
